enBad: However, even if on erev Shabbat he said that he does not want to keep it as a circumcision knife but as other knives, one can say that it does not help; for in siman 310, seif 7, in the gloss regarding a purse of money — not unless he did an action with it, that he opened it from below and removed it from the status of being set aside. And there, with a purse, it is muktzeh of monetary loss; and it is implied that speech alone on erev Shabbat does not help, only an action. What Magen Avraham wrote, siman 308 s.k. 60, regarding branches — since they stand for wood as for sitting as for wood, only he nullified his thought in fencing them for wood; thought of sitting removes it from thought of burning. It must be said that with a purse, since he designated it for money and left money in it, it is an action, and thought does not nullify it. Branches are different, for scraping is not called an action — for sitting also needs scraping, and the action is not proven upon it for burning. Thus with a circumcision knife that he circumcised with, and a slaughter knife that he slaughtered with — one can say that speech does not nullify its set-aside status unless by action. All this requires study for practical law.

enBad: Seif 1, a corpse lying in a place where one fears for it due to fire, etc. It appears to me: behold from the language of the poskim it is implied that every corpse is permitted to move because of fire or another disgrace. However behold in Midrash Rabbah parashat Vayikra chapter 5 there is, and this is its language: R' Avin said — an incident with a butcher in Tzipori who was feeding treifot and nevelot to Israel; once he ate and drank and became drunk and went up to the roof of the house and fell and died; the dogs began to lick his blood; they came and asked R' Chiyya — what is the law to remove him from before them? He said to them: it is written "and you shall be holy people to Me; flesh in the field — torn — you shall not eat, you shall throw it to the dog" — this one who was stealing vessels and feeding nevelot and treifot to Israel, etc. — from their own they are eating, end of his words; and see in Mechilta there that he explained the question was whether it is permitted to remove him from before them, etc. If so it is proven from there that for a wicked person who feeds treifot and the like, one does not desecrate Shabbat and Yom Kippur on his account to move him because of disgrace; for necessarily it deals via a loaf or a child, for without a loaf and child even if a proper person died it is forbidden; and necessarily it deals via a loaf and child; and even so they forbade to move him — and it is proven that for a wicked person we are not concerned for his disgrace. And even though one does not derive halacha from aggadah — that is only when the midrash expounds thus as halachic method or expounds not based on an incident; but when there is an actual incident and nothing in the Talmud proves the opposite, certainly we derive the law from it, since it is explicit in it that he ruled thus halacha lema'aseh. And therefore it appeared that so is the law: for a known wicked person one does not desecrate Shabbat because of his disgrace — only regarding fire and the like where there is concern that a person will be agitated over his corpse and may come to actual desecration of Shabbat — in this one does not distinguish between wicked or not; but where there is no concern he will come to d'oraisa melacha, it appears one does not desecrate Shabbat to move the corpse via a loaf and child, as explicit in the midrash mentioned, and requires study.

enBad: (21) Forbidden to salt, etc. — for that which they permit above regarding an egg to salt it is for the need of that meal; but to salt meat and an egg in order to leave for later time is similar to tanning and pickling. And behold Magen Avraham's and Taz's view is that even if his intent is to eat on that day, if it is for the need of another meal one should be careful in this [meaning when the other meal extends a long time after the first meal]; but R' Avraham sides that one forbids only if his intent is to leave until after Shabbat, and so is implied from Be'ur HaGra; and especially if the time is hot and he does so so it not spoil — certainly one may be lenient for another meal, for Taz also permits in this. Raw meat or fish — forbidden to salt it on Shabbat so it not spoil; and even in a place of loss it is forbidden; and even if he wants to salt it in order to eat it after salting while still raw — forbidden, for even though there is no tanning of foods d'oraisa, nevertheless forbidden because it appears like tanning, for salt makes the food fit and corrects it; but permitted to rinse the meat in order to eat it afterward raw, and this is not called correction, for the correction is not in the body of the meat but he rinses it because of visible blood upon it. Nevertheless it appears forbidden to rinse meat that was not salted when the third day falls on Shabbat and so it will not be forbidden afterward for cooking, since he does not want to eat it today and also there is no manner to eat raw — it is recognizable he does for weekday need; and even through a non-Jew it is forbidden to rinse, for there is not so much loss here if he does not rinse it so he can eat roasted — so wrote Magen Avraham; and it deals with an individual in his house; but a butcher who sells to others — certainly there is loss here and he may do through a non-Jew; and likewise in fattened geese that he will lose the fat if he roasts them — also according to Magen Avraham permitted through a non-Jew even an individual in his house. And even in animal meat many Acharonim agreed one may be lenient to rinse through a non-Jew, unlike Magen Avraham; and see in R' Avraham and in responsa of Noda B'Yehuda who wrote that if impossible through a non-Jew — permitted also through an Israelite; but if the meat rests in a good vessel he should wash his hands on it until the meat is soaked in water:

enBad: To set it aside. See Baer Heitev; and what Taz wrote on this — see in responsa of Peri Megadim that on the contrary, where it is better for him to salt now and it improves thereby more — there is reason to forbid on erev Shabbos; and see in Beit Yosef that even though he inclined to permit, he wrote to leave them for a short time — forbidden to salt; and so in salatin; and so if they salt in their shells the master [of the house?]; but if he puts a little oil first there is reason to permit. And what Baer Heitev wrote in the name of Magen Avraham that forbidden to rinse meat that became salted on the third day — see above siman 308; Eliyah Zuta wrote in the name of his ancestor to permit; and see in Ginas Veradim Ma'areches Shabbos siman 27: stuffed geese whose main purpose is for the fat, and in roasting the fat is entirely lost and there is loss — permitted to put water on the meat via a non-Jew; and needless to say ducks and geese fit for omtza; but even animal meat — and if impossible via a non-Jew, permitted to do via Israel; and especially if in any case he needs to wash hands on erev Shabbos; and so too in Dagul MeRevavah, and he concluded there "again I found in Eliyah Rabbah siman 308 who disputes Magen Avraham" on erev Shabbos; and in Shevut Yaakov part 3 siman 22 he wrote that Magen Avraham who is stringent applies specifically to an individual in his home, but a butcher who sells to others concedes that he can do via a non-Jew (and accordingly also in stuffed geese where there is loss of fat); and one who is stringent can tell a non-Jew to command a non-Jew, which is shvut d'shvut on erev Shabbos (and see Pri Megadim end of siman 508 regarding Yom Tov; and in Nedar Bakar siman 32 he wrote to permit on Yom Tov, and see there explicitly the words of Magen Avraham that he wrote on account of a remedy — meaning that it softens); and see in Chokhmas Adam siman 44 brought above siman 307, and in Shevut Yaakov part 2 siman 44:
